title: Female-Breadwinner Couples Are Still More Likely to Split Up
gist: Reviewing a new study of 544,911 couples across 29 affluent countries (2004-2020) by Pilar Gonalons-Pons and Allison Dunatchik, Rosemary Hopcroft reports female-breadwinner couples are 36% more likely to separate than male-breadwinner couples, all else equal. The effect persists across countries regardless of national gender norms, contradicting the long-held prediction that role-reversal instability would fade as gender norms liberalized.

insights.claim: In a study of 544,911 married and cohabiting couples across 29 affluent countries between 2004 and 2020, couples where the woman earns more than 60% of household income are more likely to separate in every country except Hungary and Cyprus.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: A near-universal cross-national pattern implies the effect is structural, not a local cultural artifact—relevant to long-run family-stability and household-formation trends.
insights.quote: couples in which the woman is the primary breadwinner—defined as earning more than 60% of the couple's total income—are more likely to separate in every country except Hungary and Cyprus
insights.locator: The issue has now been revisited

insights.claim: After controlling for both partners' education, marital versus cohabiting status, parenthood, and homeownership, female-breadwinner couples were 36% more likely to separate than male-breadwinner couples, and equal-earner couples about 6% more likely.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: The effect survives standard controls, so it is not explained by the usual confounders—strengthening the claim that it is a real behavioral driver of dissolution.
insights.quote: Female-breadwinner couples were 36% more likely to separate than male-breadwinner couples, all else equal.

insights.claim: The elevated separation risk applies similarly to married and cohabiting couples, even though cohabiting couples separate more overall.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: The breadwinner effect is independent of relationship formality, indicating it operates on the underlying partnership dynamic.
insights.quote: the increase in separation risk associated with having a female breadwinner was similar for both married and cohabiting couples

insights.claim: For decades sociologists predicted that women's economic success would erode the male-breadwinner norm and make female-breadwinner instability disappear, treating higher separation rates as a product of social disapproval over violated gender norms.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: Establishes the consensus prediction the new data falsifies, framing the finding as against-consensus.
insights.quote: As women became more economically successful, they argued, people generally would become more accepting of role reversals within the household

insights.claim: The study was co-authored by Pilar Gonalons-Pons, one of the authors of a widely discussed 2016 study that had reported female-breadwinner divorce risk was no longer true for recent marriage cohorts—and the new findings reverse that earlier conclusion.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: An author revising her own prior finding lends unusual credibility to the reversal, signaling the earlier optimistic view was wrong.
insights.quote: The issue has now been revisited by one of the authors of the 2016 study, Pilar Gonalons-Pons

insights.claim: Female-breadwinner couples separated more regardless of national gender norms—including the share endorsing male-breadwinner beliefs or supporting dual-earner marriages—and the association did not vary with the gender wage gap, prevalence of female-breadwinner couples, or women's educational advantage.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: Ruling out macro gender-equality measures removes the leading explanation and points toward deeper, less policy-tractable causes.
insights.quote: Female-breadwinner couples were more likely to separate regardless of the proportion of people in the country who endorsed traditional beliefs or supported dual-earner marriages
insights.locator: National Gender Norms or Other Factors?

insights.claim: Among couples with dependent children, female-breadwinner couples were 49% more likely to separate than male-breadwinner couples, versus a 23% higher risk among those without children.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: Children amplify the instability, suggesting work-family conflict is a key mechanism—though the study says it does not fully explain the effect.
insights.quote: female-breadwinner couples with children were 49% more likely to separate than male-breadwinner couples, a much higher rate than the 23% higher risk of separation faced by female breadwinner-couples without children

insights.claim: The study found little support for alternative explanations—that female-breadwinner instability stems from women's financial independence, women raising earnings in anticipation of divorce, husband unemployment, or household financial hardship.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: Eliminating economic-mechanism explanations narrows the plausible causes toward preference/psychology-based accounts.
insights.quote: Female-breadwinner couples were not substantially less stable because women had greater financial independence
insights.locator: The study likewise found little support

insights.claim: Marriages in which the wife earns more than the husband rose from about 5% of married couples in 1972 to roughly 16% today, a trend the author expects to continue as young women outnumber men in universities and dominate many professional occupations.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: A rising share of couples exposed to elevated instability implies growing aggregate divorce/separation pressure as women's earnings keep climbing.
insights.quote: rising from about 5% of married couples in 1972 to roughly 16% today
insights.locator: This reflects a broader social trend.

insights.claim: The author argues evolutionary psychology best explains the persistence—sex differences in mate preferences shaped over human evolution continue to influence modern relationships—so the instability reflects enduring psychological predispositions rather than social norms and is unlikely to vanish as societies become more gender-egalitarian.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: If the driver is evolved preference rather than culture, the trend is durable and resistant to policy or attitudinal change.
insights.quote: this is because sex differences in mate preferences, shaped over humanity's long evolutionary history, continue to influence modern relationships

insights.claim: As a cultural illustration, the author cites that Taylor Swift earned at least four times as much as NFL star Travis Kelce last year with a far higher net worth, reflecting the broader rise of wives out-earning husbands.
insights.speaker: Rosemary L. Hopcroft
insights.so_what: A high-profile example that anchors the abstract trend in a widely known couple, useful for gauging cultural salience.
insights.quote: Pop superstar Taylor Swift earned at least four times as much as NFL star Travis Kelce last year and her net worth is much higher than his.
